text.p: European aircraft consortium Airbus expects to make a decision on whether to go ahead with its planned 550-seat A3XX towards the end of 1998 or in 1999, managing director Jean Pierson said on Thursday.
"The decisive year is next year," he told journalists at Airbus's headquarters in southwest France.
The aim is to have the plane enter service in 2003, he added.

Two airlines have advised Airbus that Boeing has told them that it is poised to launch a new large plane as soon as Airbus is close to announcing a launch of the A3XX, to "cut the ground from under Airbus", Pierson said.
The A3XX is a strategic product for Airbus, needed to break Boeing's monopoly at the large capacity segment and to realise its aim of winning a half share of the world market by 2002.
Airbus has 800 staff working on the A3XX, as well employees at its partners. Airbus is a consortium made up France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace and Spain's Casa.

The decision to seek partners outside the Airbus consortium to work on the A3XX stemmed from the trend to globalisation in the aerospace industry, a desire to share risk and a restructuring of the Italian industry, Pierson said.
The Italian government has recently consolidated its aerospace industry around Alenia, a unit of Finmeccanica . Alenia has agreed to participate in the A3XX project.
It was important to bring Alenia, which is not an Airbus partner, closer to the European industry rather than let it get closer to the United States, Pierson said.
Alenia is a subcontractor to McDonnell Douglas, which is merging with Boeing to create a industrial giant with annual sales of $50 billion.
Boeing wants to retain its monopoly in the large capacity segment seating more than 400 passengers, with its 747 jumbo jet, while spending as little as possible, Pierson said.

Its strategy consisted of offering a derivative of the 747, codenamed 747X, but that failed to win launch customers, he said. Boeing was now saying there was insufficient demand for a new large plane, to put off Airbus from attacking its monopoly.

But Airbus forecasts potential sales of 1,400 planes seating over 400 over the next 20 years and, in support, cites Boeing's Current Market Outlook, published in March 1996, which forecasts demand for 1,600 planes for this category. The Airbus forecast represents 25 percent of total dollar sales for all aircraft types, and Boeing's estimate 23 percent.
All of Airbus's actions, including its planned status change to a limited liability company, are aimed at gaining a half share of the world market, Pierson said.

That strategy includes expanding the product range at the low capacity end, with the 100-seater passenger jet to be built with China and Singapore, as well as extending the A340 long-range jet through derivatives.
Airbus wants to launch the longer range A340-500 and the stretched A340-600 variants to round out the A340 four engine wide-body plane.

But a launch decision on the A340-600, which would seat 375 passengers, is being held up while Airbus negotiates an engine supply agreement with Rolls Royce Plc, Pratt & Whitney, a United Technologies Corp unit, and Snecma.
Differences over price concessions with General Electric for an exclusive supply agreement led to the lapsing of an exclusive period of negotiations.
